Good morning, Excellencies, distinguished guests, dear colleagues. It's my distinct honor and pleasure to welcome you to this AREA Formula meeting entitled Safeguarding Education in Sudan, Investing in Peace and Recovery. We thank our E3+ partners co-members and the DRC and Liberia for their co-sponsorship and steadfast commitment to this agenda. This meeting comes at a time when Sudan's education system faces unprecedented challenges. Since April 2023, conflict has uprooted millions of children from their classrooms and attacks on educational infrastructure has surged. In this crisis, Education must remain a neutral, protected space, guided by always by the best interests of the child. Education is not a right, but a lifeline and a cornerstone of Sudan's recovery. Today, we look forward to shedding light and on discussing concrete steps to ensure safe, inclusive and continuous learning for every Sudanese child, even mine, even amid conflict. Excellencies, distinguished guests, dear colleagues, we welcome the Deputy Secretary-General, Her Excellency Ms. Amina Mohamed, and our distinguished briefers to this meeting. I am pleased to give the floor to Madam Amina Mohamed, Deputy Secretary-General. You have the floor.

Thank you, Your Excellency, Mr. Abakar Dahir Osman, the Permanent Representative of the Federal Republic of Somalia to the UN. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, and friends, my deep appreciation to you, Ambassador Osman, and to Somalia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Liberia for bringing this issue before the Council. 1,210 days, that's how long this war has gone on for. Long enough for 33 million people, more than half of Sudan, to need humanitarian aid to survive. Long enough for famine to take hold and four million women and children to face acute malnourishment this year. Long enough for Sudan to become the largest displacement crisis in the world, nearly nine million people driven from their homes inside the country and millions more forced to cross its borders. Long enough for cholera, measles, dengue and hepatitis E to move through camps where families have already fled two, three, four times over. Long enough for the atrocities of sexual violence to be used again and again and again as a horrific weapon against women and girls. Long enough for more than 17 million Sudanese children to need humanitarian assistance. Long enough for mass killings and sexual violence in villages, of rape and gang rape, of abduction and trafficking of children recruited and detained. This war has to end and it has to end now. Those who committed these crimes must answer for them and the rule of law must prevail in Sudan. States beyond Sudan's borders continue to fuel the fire of this conflict by facilitating the flow of deadly weapons. Their actions are deepening and prolonging the suffering of the people, mothers, young girls and children of Sudan. This must cease immediately. The United Nations will put the full weight of its capacity behind every pathway to peace. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, among everything this war is taking, one of the most significant is the future of Sudan depriving the education of its children. Today, at least eight million school-age children remain out of school, with a disproportionate impact on millions of displaced children, especially those seeking refuge outside of Sudan. Darfur alone has seen nearly three-quarters of its schools damaged, destroyed, or otherwise rendered non-functional since the onset of the conflict. Five children in every six are out of school, and many parents will tell you they would rather keep their children at home than send them to a classroom. because home for them is the only place left where they can keep them safe. Since 2024, the United Nations has verified more than 67 attacks on schools across Sudan, while over 154 instances of military use of schools have been reported. These figures represent only documented incidents, while the true scale of attacks on schools is undoubtedly much greater. Shelling and airstrikes continue to damage schools and endanger children, while incidents of looting and arson of schools, as well as threats against educational personnel, have been extensively reported. Attacks against schools are frontal assaults on children's safety, their dignity. They lose protective spaces, opportunities to develop socially with their peers, and access to essential services such as the school feeding programs, health care, and mental health support. As we have seen time and time again, how prolonged disruptions in education disproportionately affect girls and young women. More than half of Sudan's teachers have gone unpaid, yet many of them are still teaching against all odds. The national examinations are now out of reach for students across large parts of Darfur and Kordofan. Parallel exams are being planned in the five Darfur states, raising real concerns about whether those certificates would be recognized. It is essential that all children, whether in areas affected by conflict, displacement settings, or more stable locations, have access to the same nationally recognized examinations, the same quality education. A unified exam helps ensure fairness, protects the value of students' qualifications, Without one, a generation of Sudanese youth leave schools with no open doors, no university placing, no training, no job. Those are the children at risk that armed groups recruit and become our child soldiers. I could read numbers to you for the whole of the five minutes I've been given and still fall short of what has been done to Sudan's children, especially its girls. Sudan has already lost a generation to earlier wars and is losing another one now. This year, with our partners, we have brought more than a million Sudanese children back into some form of learning, but it's simply just not enough. This is a war that men have started, but it is being paid for on the backs of women and on the backs of children who have no say in any of it, but suffer the worst consequences. It is time to stop the war and to pull Sudan back from the brink of losing another generation of its children. Excellencies, colleagues and friends, The members of the Security Council must do their utmost to bring this conflict to an end, to create the conditions for peace and the enabling environment for Sudan's children to return to learning. I urge you to do everything within your power to do so, for the young Sudanese living through this war today, and for future generations who will inherit whatever is left of their country. Education is both life-saving, it's life-changing. It protects children today and lays the foundation for peace, recovery and stability tomorrow. Education is hope, hope in a future that may seem impossibly distant. Just as in Gaza, parents know that they may not live to see peace in their country, but one day their child just might do so. And that education is what will let them rebuild peace, prosperity in their country so that they may have the right to thrive in it. Sudan's children have waited 1,210 days for the war to end. They should not have to wait any longer. Thank you.
I thank the Deputy Secretary-General for her remarks. I now invite Ms. Hanan Suleiman, Deputy Executive Director of UNICEF, to provide her briefing.

Excellencies, thank you to Ambassador Bakarr Dahir Ousman for convening today's Arya Formula meeting, and to Liberia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo for co-sponsoring this very important discussion. Excellencies, we meet today against the backdrop of a devastating conflict that has now entered its fourth year, a conflict where children's education continues to be under attack. In my remarks today, I will focus on three things. the challenges of children and education in Sudan, how progress is possible when resources and political will are available, and what you as member states can do to protect children and education in Sudan. Since the Security Council adopted Resolution 2736 in 2024, calling among others for the protection of civilians and for compliance by all parties to conflict with international law, The United Nations has verified across Sudan more than 67 attacks on schools, while over 154 instances of military use of schools in Sudan have been reported, as just communicated by our Deputy Secretary General. These figures represent only documented incidences, while the true scale of attacks on schools is undoubtedly much greater. Darfur alone has seen nearly three quarters, 73%, of its schools damaged, destroyed, or otherwise rendered nonfunctional since the onset of the conflict in April 2023. The use of explosive weapons by parties to the conflict in populated areas remains a leading cause of damage to and destruction of schools. In Sudan, armed drones have emerged as a major means of deploying explosive weapons, causing extensive damage to schools and inflicting grave harm to children. During the first four months alone of this year, nearly 80% of reported child casualties were attributed to attacks involving armed drones. At the same time, shelling and airstrikes continue to damage schools and endanger children. while incidents of looting and arson of schools, as well as threats against education personnel have been extensively reported. Since the outbreak of the war, Sudan consistently ranks as the country with the highest number of out-of-school children in the world. Today, at least 8 million school-age children remain out of school, including approximately 4.1 million girls. with a disproportionate impact on millions of displaced children, notably those seeking refuge outside of Sudan. Further, nearly half of Sudan's school buildings can no longer function as classrooms. In addition to the widespread displacement of education personnel, the conflict has halted the salaries of many teachers, particularly in Darfur and Kordofan, thereby severely affecting their livelihood and the continuity of learning. Children's access to education is not only threatened by direct attack on schools or education personnel, but by the secondary impact on education from the collapse of the infrastructure that keeps schools running. For instance, a school relies on access to electricity, water, sanitation, and hygiene to function. Last year, a strike on energy infrastructure in the White Nile state cut off the electricity needed to operate a major water treatment facility. As a result, schools lost access to both energy and water, forcing their closure, with tens of thousands of students losing access to education. Attacks against schools are not only grave violations against children, they are frontal assaults on children's safety, dignity, and future. When schools are attacked, occupied, or rendered unsafe, children lose far more than learning opportunities. They lose protective spaces, opportunities to develop socially with their peers, and access to essential services such as school feeding, health care, and mental health support. Their vulnerabilities also surge when they miss out on life-saving information taught within the classroom. For example, in Sudan, learning about the risks posed by explosive remnants of war are a lifeline that teachers provide. Children who are out of school also face significantly heightened protection risks, including exploitation, child labor, child marriage, trafficking, and recruitment into armed forces and armed groups. Excellencies, education is both life-saving and life-changing. Despite the challenges outlined above, progress is still possible with political will and adequate resources. UNICEF continues to work with partners nationwide to restore safe learning environments, distribute education supplies, and advocate for unified, accessible national examinations for all students regardless of locations. Three illustrative initiatives include, In May 2026, UNICEF and Save the Children, with support from the Global Partnership for Education, launched the Building Resilience to Improve Development and Growth in Education in Sudan, bridges. The new program will help more than 328,000 conflict-affected children to return to learning across Sudan by restoring access to education in some of the hardest-hit areas, and in supporting longer term recovery of the national education system. Investment in the national system is an absolute must. Approximately 850 schools are expected to reopen through this initiative across seven conflict affected states. Secondly, last year, hundreds of primary schools across Brunei state benefited from a UNICEF and partner led enrollment campaign that also provided essential teaching materials to enhance lesson delivery and improve learning for displaced and vulnerable children. Guided by the principle of leaving no child behind, the all inclusive approach With the support of the European Union and other partners, more than 170,000 children across all 418 schools in Blue Nile alone had access to safe and quality education. The program succeeded in a major increase in enrollment of displaced children, including refugees, and ensured that they learned side by side with children from host communities, fostering social cohesion and healing. Third, prolonged disruptions in education have disproportionately affected girls and young women, with many facing barriers to accessing employment. As a result, in White Nile, the Prospects Partnership, a program implemented by ILO, UNHCR, and UNICEF, is expanding access to technical and vocational training, apprenticeship and youth engagement programs, and equipping young people with market-relevant skills to shape their futures. Beyond vocational training, the program also strengthens access to rights, supporting inclusive national systems, and helping young people move into education and employment pathways while fostering social cohesion. Today, El Sefira village in White Nile is home to hundreds of skilled young people, electricians, tailors, technicians, and mechanics, who are now earning an income and contributing to their communities. These are important examples, but much more must be done to reach the millions of children whose rights to education have been denied. This is just a small drop. Excellencies, I would like to leave you with four requests. First, UNICEF is urging all member states to demand an immediate ceasefire in Sudan, that all parties to the conflict in Sudan respect international humanitarian law and end and prevent grave violations against children. This also includes signing and fully implementing the United Nations Children and Armed Conflict Action Plans. Member States should also support Sudan to implement the Safe Schools Declaration, including the adoption of policies that protect schools, learners and educators, while ensuring accountability for grave rights violations. Education should and must be systematically integrated into national action plans on children in armed conflict to reduce the exposure of vulnerable children and to reintegrate affected children during post-conflict recovery. Secondly, member states should also provide sustained and flexible financing to guarantee safe, inclusive, and quality education in Sudan. This supports children affected by armed conflict to continue learning as quickly as possible. Third, Sudanese stakeholders, member states, including members of this esteemed council, and all concerned stakeholders should take action to ensure that education in Sudan remains a neutral space that is protected from politicization and division. It is essential that all children, whether in areas affected by conflict, displacement settings, or more stable locations, have access to the same nationally recognized examinations. A unified exam helps ensure fairness, protects the value of student qualifications, and avoids divisions that could limit their future opportunities. Excellencies, education protects children today and helps build the foundations for peace tomorrow. With that in mind, I would like to close by urging you to unequivocally denounce attacks on education across Sudan, to reaffirm that military use of schools are never acceptable and must never be normalized, to consistently call for accountability when attacks take place, and to use the influence you hold with parties to armed conflict to help protect the children of Sudan and their education. We urgently need your action to end this conflict. Without a political resolution and lasting peace, humanitarian, including educational needs, will continue to outpace the response by far, and children's suffering will deepen. Safe education is more than an investment in the prosperous future of Sudan. It is a vital protection measure and a cornerstone of sustainable peace. It is a fundamental right that every child in Sudan must enjoy. The choices made by this council can help ensure that children carry books instead of burdens and hope instead of harm. Thank you very much.
I thank Ms. Sulaiman for her briefings and now invite Ms. Lisa Chang-Bender, Executive Director of Global Coalition to Protect Education from Attack, to provide her briefings.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I thank Somalia for convening this meeting and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Liberia for co-sponsoring it. As noted, Sudan remains the country with the highest number of out-of-school children in the world. However, new figures are even more troubling. Education Cannot Wait released in June figures that put the number at 12.3 million children out of school. My organization, the Global Coalition to Protect Education from Attack, welcomed Sudan as one of the earliest endorsers of the Safe Schools Declaration in 2015, and we stand ready to support Sudan, this Council, and all present because Sudan cannot build without a commitment to education. GCPA has tracked attacks on education for 15 years. In our last report, we found 88 countries were affected by attacks on education. This is a global problem. And let me emphasize what we have learned over the years. Attacks on schools are not just the heartbreaking deaths of children in places where they should be safest. It is not just the destruction of one of the largest infrastructure investments that countries can make, or the killing, maiming, and terrorizing of teachers who are the largest civil servant cadre in countries. The attacks have lasting harm that go beyond these immediate devastations. To name just a few, they suppress enrollment, they contribute to child marriage. These are not trends that are easily changed and disproportionately affect girls. They also create lasting toxic stress, which have horrible negative consequences for children throughout their lives and development. We must be committed to their safety and well-being. GCPA's independent monitoring identifies Sudan as one of the most heavily affected countries in the world by attacks on education. And in our analysis, we found two patterns. First, schools sheltering the displaced are being struck again and again. In 2025 alone, Balak Girls School, just an hour before classes started, was bombed in March. Drone strikes hit two sheltering schools in Kordofan on consecutive days in June. And in December, a drone struck a kindergarten in Kalouji, killing 32 children, and then targeted the paramedics that arrived to help. The second pattern, educators are being targeted. not just for where they work, but for who they serve. In June 2025, mass graves contained tortured students and teachers was discovered in Wad Madani. Through August and September, GCPEA documented teachers arrested in Darfur over alleged ties to the Port Sudan government. These same teachers that we've already acknowledged are going without pay and are doing so much to help the children of Sudan. However, sharing this evidence only matters if it leads to action. Accountability is protection. It is a critical form of deterrence. Every investigation, every sanction that names education as a protected infrastructure, every case brought before this council makes Sudan's schools safer not only today, but tomorrow. The case to act now is also a peace and recovery case. Education inequality groups I'm sorry, education inequality between groups roughly doubles the risk of conflict, while greater gender equality in education lowers it by as much as 37%. This is why GCPEA is gravely concerned about the exam crisis. This April, over 280,000 students, and you can only imagine what they've been through, went to travel to take their exams. 60% of them were girls and were not able to access exam sites. Subsequently, a parallel process has been announced for exams in RSF controlled areas. I'd like to draw your attention to two recent studies, UNDP ISS Africa's Beyond the Conflict and the Government of Sudan and UNESCO's Sudan Price of Inaction Report. Both of these reports agree that disrupted schooling carries a steep economic cost, degrading the workforce and entrenching generational poverty. If conflict persists, By 2043, GDP will be $34.5 billion lower. But if the war ends and education is protected, GDP could instead reach $58.2 billion, even outperforming some of its African income peers. Failure to invest in education will perpetuate a vicious cycle, more conflict, more poverty. Protecting and investing in education will promote a virtuous cycle, more peace, more prosperity. So let me close with some practical recommendations. First, on a political level, education and protection appeals must be funded immediately. The 84% funding gap is shameful. Second, we echo and build on UNICEF's call to integrate education into Sudan's national action plan and also urge the group of friends on children in armed conflict in Sudan be reestablished with an explicit focus on attacks on education. On a technical level, verification bodies and accountability mechanisms must capture data on attacks on education as distinct category of harm. Finally, we echo the call for a single national guaranteed mechanism for Sudanese examinations and certification so that today's students are not divided by where the front line falls. Excellencies, Sudan's children have not stopped asking for the chance to learn, even as their schools are struck, their teachers killed, their futures deferred. This council can answer that request with protection because where education is protected, children are safer and peace has room to grow. Thank you so much.

I thank Ms. Bender for her briefings. Colleagues, before we proceed, I should mention that the DSG, Deputy Secretary General, Her Excellency Ms. Amina Mohamed has other commitments. We express our gratitude for her participation and invaluable contribution. I propose we allow her to depart now to attend other meetings. Thank you. Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished guests and colleagues, education is often described as foundation of development. Today, we gather to recognize another equally important truth. Education is also foundation for peace. At the heart of every society that has rebuilt from conflict lies the same enduring force, education. Education has enabled communities to recover, rebuild public institutions, and prepare new generations to lead their nations towards stability and prosperity. For decades, Sudan stood as one of Africa's and the Arab region's leading center of learning, with reputation that extended well beyond its borders. Its schools and universities educated generations of students from across Africa and beyond, many of whom returned to their countries to contribute to national development, institution building, and public services. In doing so, Sudan's education system made a lasting contribution not only to the development of its own people, but also to the institution building, human capital development, and regional cooperation across Africa and the wider region. Today, however, the conflict has interrupted Sudan's ability to carry that legacy forward. The conflict has disrupted the educations of millions of children. Schools have been damaged, destroyed, or rendered inaccessible, teachers have been displaced, many young people have seen their education interrupted at the defining moment in their lives. The consequence extend far beyond classroom. Every year of lost learning weakens human capital, increases children's vulnerability to recruitment and exploitation, and narrows the opportunity for recovery when peace returns. At the same time, this conflict has raised another important challenge, preserving the integrity of Sudan's national education system. A unified national education system is more than curriculum, examinations, or certificates. It's an institution that binds a nation together. It provides continuity, reinforces national identity, and ensures that every child, regardless of where they live, share a common educational foundation. Its preservation will be essential to Sudan's future recovery and national cohesion. This is why safeguarding education must go beyond protecting school buildings. It must also include protecting students, teachers, and educational personnel, ensuring safe and continuous access to learning, preserving the integrity of Sudan's national recognized education system, and preventing fragmentation through parallel educational structures that risk undermining national cohesion and the credibility of the educational qualification for future generations. We support the Secretary General as a personal envoy, Haristo's effort in this regard. When we protect education, we do more than safeguard the rights of children, we safeguard the future of societies. Excellencies, colleagues, The Security Council has consistently recognized the importance of protecting children affected by armed conflict, civilians, and infrastructures. Today's discussion invites us to consider how education contributes not only to the child protection, but also the resilience, institution building, and sustainable development and sustainable peace. In this context, ensuring accountability for crimes and upholding obligations to international humanitarian law are essential. We must also address the actions of external actors who fuel the war, including the implementation of arms embargo to stem the flow of weapons and increment drones that threatens the safety of the schools and communities. It's equally important to engage fully in the political process for a ceasefire, own ceasefire and support the government in its Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned political process. Only by advancing those efforts can we create the conditions necessary for education to thrive. It's also encourages us to reflect on practical ways in which the international community can support these efforts through stronger protection of schools, sustained support for Sudanese education sector, assistance to displaced learners, and cooperation aimed at preserving the country's national education system for future generations. Ultimately, the question before us is not simply to restore education after conflict, it's how to ensure that education continues despite conflict so that when peace comes, Sudan will have a generation prepared not only to shape the country's future, but to rebuild it. It's our hope that today's discussion will generate practical ideas, strengthen international cooperation, and reaffirm our shared commitment to ensuring that every Sudanese child retain the opportunity to learn, to grow, and to contribute to a peaceful and prosperous Sudan. I thank you again. I now give the floor to the council members. And I'll begin giving the floor to the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Mr. President, the Democratic Republic of the Congo would like to congratulate Somalia for organizing this area formula. which we were honored to co-sponsor alongside Liberia. We would also like to thank Madam Deputy Secretary General of the United Nations, as well as the Deputy Executive Director of UNICEF, the Executive Director of the Global Coalition to Protect Education from Attack as well. The conflict raging in Sudan since April 2023 continues to place a heavy burden on civilians, and the most vulnerable of them are children. While the human losses, forced displacement and humanitarian needs indeed garner all the attention of the international community, attacks on the education system is also a major threat for the future of the country whose day-to-day life can hear is marked by the sound of weapons going off. Schools are being closed. and learning has been interrupted. This is depriving millions of Sudanese children not only of their fundamental right to education but also of a safe space, a space of stability and hope. Indeed, the history of conflict shows sufficiently that when a school closes, it is not simply learning that is interrupted, it is also a barrier against recruitment, exploitation and other violations that we can stop if stopping a school from closing. The conflict in Sudan and the ongoing violence. pose a great risk to this plural society that has already been sorely tested. Beyond the immediate urgency, this crisis could also leave an imprint on the social fabric of Sudan, and this is something that we should bear in mind. For the younger generations who are growing up in this context, the consequences of this war will not only be measured in the number of schools destroyed or school years lost. It will also be measured in the lasting trace that this will lead on a whole generation of young Sudanese people who will then need to ensure the recovery of their country. They will continue to be deprived of education and they will not have any prospects for empowerment, jobs, participation in public life. This will all be compromised. Beyond the human tragedy that this represents. Being out of school for a long time erodes human capital inevitably, and this human capital is needed to rebuild institutions, rebuild social coherence, and it is needed to consolidate lasting peace. Although they're on the front line of this war, Sudanese children are also its greatest hope, and therefore the way in which they'll be protected taught and supported today will determine the capacity of Sudan to recover and to build lasting peace. Preserving education for these children is therefore an imperative for the international community. Indeed, preserving, protecting education and safeguarding education in Sudan is protecting, safeguarding women and men who have the responsibility to build a more prosperous, peaceful future for their country. President, the experience of the DRC shows that protecting and safeguarding education is not something that should happen after a conflict is resolved. It is one of the conditions for the resolution to a conflict. This is why my government My government of my country rolled out a law in 2009 protecting children and we also have a framework law from 2014 for national education system. This legislation creates our national strategy for education in emergencies. This legal arsenal aims to ensure continuity and the protection of learning whether this be formal or informal. It also seeks to guarantee the safety of students and staff and provide psycho social support in response to conflicts and disasters. Our approach therefore brings together continuity of learning, institutional resilience and peace building. This choice stems from a simple conviction: crises should never condemn an entire generation to have its education interrupted. Preserving the education system is preserving and maintaining the capacity of a nation to train its citizens of tomorrow. It will strengthen its institutions and it will consolidate lasting peace. In this connection, the DRC welcomes the efforts made by the African Union for to protect education in situations of crisis, particularly through initiatives from the Peace and Security Council and also the African Union Center for the Education of Girls and Women in Africa. These initiatives show the will of our continent to make education not only a fundamental right, but also a tool for resilience, recovery and peace building. Thus, it merits to be fully supported and strengthened. However, As determining as national policies are for ensuring continuity of education, they cannot replace lasting protection for children. And that this cessation of hostilities is key here. While that has not happened, schools will be exposed, teachers will be displaced, and thousands of children will be deprived of their right to learn. This is why the DRC reiterates its appeal for an immediate cessation of hostilities. safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access, as well as a political dialogue that is sincere and inclusive between parties. Only a political solution will create the conditions that are necessary to rebuild the education system, to support national recovery and will allow for lasting peace. With this in mind, we encourage the international community, alongside regional actors, to strengthen their support to the Sudanese authorities to protect the entire national education system to ensure continuous learning and protect schools against any use that is not compatible with their civilian vocation, and also to support teachers. whose commitment remains essential to preserve the human capital of Sudan. These efforts must be part of a global approach bringing together humanitarian action, development and peace building, so that education remains a real tool for resilience and stability. President, in conclusion, for the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the question that brings us together today goes beyond simply access to education. It invites us to think about what trace this war will leave on future generations and what actions we can take collectively to protect it. We have the collective responsibility to ensure that Sudanese children don't become a generation defined by the conflict, but a generation that is prepared to lead the recovery of their country. And this is why investing today in education is investing in peace, recovery and stability of the Sudan of tomorrow. Thank you.

I thank the representative of Democratic Republic of Congo. for her remarks. And before I give the floor to Liberia, I want to recognize both Democratic Republic of Congo and Liberia as the co-sponsors of this AREA formula. I thank you again on behalf of the Federal Government of Somalia, and now give the floor to the representative of Liberia.

Liberia's history makes it imperative and dutiful for Liberia to join its E3 colleagues, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Somalia to co-host this Area Formula meeting on safeguarding education in Sudan, investing in peace, recovery and stability. Liberia thanks the briefers. Hana Suleiman, Deputy Executive Director of UNICEF, and Lisa Chung-Bender, Executive Director of the Global Coalition to Protect Education from Attack, who briefed us. We also want to thank in absentia the Deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations, Anna J. Mohammed, for honoring this occasion. The adverse effects of war do not dissipate when guns fall silent. Its deepest wounds are carried by a child, and that wound, left untreated, bleeds across generations. You have heard the grim statistics 17 million children affected by this war and some 8 million are out of school. Schools have been bombed, occupied, and abandoned. Teachers unpaid, examinations disrupted. Sudan is not only losing ground to a war, it is losing a generation and may lose generations if this war does not come to an end. The law is clear. Schools are protected civilian objects. Resolution 2601 condemns attacks on education and demands an end to the military use of schools. Liberia calls on all parties to honor these obligations, implement the Safe Schools Declaration, and cooperate fully with the UN's monitoring and reporting mechanism. A school is a sanctuary. Never a barrack and never a target. Mr. Chair, Liberia knows the cost from lived experience. Our civil conflict did not only destroy buildings. It drove our teachers, doctors, engineers, and professionals into exile. for many, many years. When peace returned, we confronted a painful truth. An entire generation had come of age without formal education or vocational training. They became parents without the tools to educate their own children, passing deprivation forward. An uneducated electorate then voted as their conditions shaped them, evaluating leaders ill-equipped to govern. Unskilled and underemployed youth became the most vulnerable class in the nation, easily recruited by armed groups and criminal networks, not for lack of virtue. But because despite the orders, but because desperation is the oldest recruitment tool in history, we are still healing from these wounds. Our recovery taught us a hard truth. Rebuilding a nation does not begin at the ballot box. It begins at the blackboard. Where classrooms close, demagogues recruit. Every child kept in school is one less child available to an armed group and one more citizen capable of building peace. Liberia therefore calls for action on three fronts. First, protect schools. endorse the Safe School Declaration and embed in it domestic law, military doctrine, and rules of engagement. Second, keep children learning, preserve examinations and certification, expand offline and accelerated learning, guarantee girls equal access, Provide psychological support. Displacement must never mean disconnection from a future. Third, Liberia acts. That education be funded as the foundation of recovery. Scale up financing through education cannot wait. And Sudan's humanitarian response plan. Pay teachers living salaries. Invest in skills and livelihoods for adolescents who have already lost years. The cost of education is always less than the cost of the war that follows its absence. Liberia says accountability must follow. Attacks on schools, students, and teachers may constitute war crimes. There can be no impunity from those who make war on children's future. Mr. Chair, working with the African Union, IGAC, and the United Nations, Liberia will keep education at the center of students' path to peace. Peace is measured not only by silent guns, but by children learning in safety, teachers teaching without fear, and young people entering adulthood with the capacity to build rather than the vulnerability to destroy. The generation Sudan saves today will determine the Sudan that governs tomorrow. Every child kept in a classroom is a vote cast for peace across every election, every generation, and every decade to come. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Liberia for his statement and now give the floor to the representative of Greece.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. We would like to thank Somalia for convening today's ARYA Formula meeting, as well as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Liberia for co-sponsoring this important initiative. We also thank Her Excellency Ms. Amina Mohamed, Deputy Secretary-General, for her remarks, and the distinguished briefers for their valuable presentations. Today's discussion is both timely and critical. Safeguarding education is not only a humanitarian imperative, it is also a prerequisite for sustainable peace, recovery and long-term stability. When schools are destroyed, occupied or forced to close, children lose opportunities for learning and communities lose one of the strongest foundations for resilience and lasting peace. Nowhere is this more evident than in Sudan, where children continue to bear a disproportionate share of the conflict's devastating consequences. According to the Secretary-General's latest report on children and armed conflict, the United Nations verified 1,889 grave violations affecting 1,681 children in 2025. More than 1,300 children were killed or maimed, while others were subjected to sexual violence, abduction, and recruitment by armed groups. Particularly alarming are credible reports of child recruitment through digital platforms, especially social media. Attacks against schools increased by an alarming 57% compared to the previous reporting period, while schools continue to be used for military purposes. More broadly, Sudan's education system has been severely disrupted. More than 17 million children have experienced serious disruption to their education. Nearly 8 million remain out of school. Almost half of school buildings are no longer functional and more than 7,000 schools are located in active conflict areas.
